instructions:
You are reading the plain-language text of a codebase map. A reader meets each field ALONE, inside one box, with no paragraph around it, and does not read code.

Judge ONLY these two things:
  1. UNKNOWN WORD — a term the reader has not met and the field does not explain. Product words and words already in the map's Glossary are fine; jargon, an internal codename, or an unexplained abbreviation is not.
  2. LOST PRECISION — the sentence is short and plain but says nothing specific. "The system checks the user" is the shape: grammatical, readable, and it names no decision, no data and no actor. This is the worse failure, because it looks correct.

Do NOT report sentence length, em dashes, code names or an opening "It" — those are counted deterministically and the lead already has the numbers.
Be conservative. Report a field only when you can say WHICH word is unknown, or WHAT the sentence should have said. If in doubt, pass the field.

For each field you flag, return its `where` exactly as given, one of `unknown word` or `lost precision`, and one short line naming the word or the missing specific.

fields.text: A pass that left statements unchecked is refused until the operator declares that stopping early was deliberate. The declaration must name what was checked first.
A pass that stopped early and a pass whose checkers died look identical from inside the tool. Without the declaration the map cannot say which happened.
How much of a map was checked is counted against the statement list as it stood before any fixes. Statements nobody voted on stay in that list.
Counting against the fixed map shows nothing was ever disproved. The disproved statements are exactly the ones the fixes removed.
A statement the checkers disproved may not remain in the map word for word. A run that finds one fails.
The map would keep asserting something its own checkers proved wrong. Every count in the testing record would still read clean.
Correcting the code link under a statement never counts against the statement itself. The check that finds a moved link reports it and never fails a run.
If a moved line read as a disproof, ordinary code moves would make a true map look wrong. The real defects would drown in the noise.
What coyodex does next is decided by the working tree, never by what the project's history still holds.
A person who deleted the map to start fresh gets the old map handed back instead.
Before any work starts, the person is told which files will be read and what the pin means.
Whole folders can be left out of the map, and nobody ever learns they were skipped.
A rebuild never opens the map it is replacing, so the new map cannot copy the old one.
Two maps that agree because one copied the other read as confirmation, and the old mistakes survive.
A map built on uncommitted code records a commit marked as not containing that code.
A pin that hides uncommitted code sends every later reader, and every later comparison, to the wrong lines.
Nothing the user owns is committed, stashed or overwritten unless the user asks for it.
A reviewed map, or a commit the person never intended, is lost, and coyodex cannot undo either.
Clearing the way for a rebuild files the old map away instead of deleting it.
A deleted map takes its recorded exceptions and corrections with it, and nothing can rebuild them.
A review of a build is refused while anything is still writing that build's map.
A report about a half-written map describes a run that has not happened yet.

The map server answers only the person sitting at this machine. It listens on the loopback address and nowhere else. A request that names any other site is refused. A request that changes the remembered project list must carry a private marker header.
Without this limit, a web page open in the reader's browser could read the whole project's source code.

The server shows only project folders the user has opened before. It never searches the disk for maps. An address naming any other project is refused. A folder can be added only when it already holds a coyodex folder.
Without this limit, a page could name any folder on the machine and read the code inside it.

The code viewer opens a file only when it sits inside the project being shown. A path that climbs out of the project is refused. A link that points outside the project is refused too. From the working tree only files version control accounts for are served.
Without this limit, a reader could pull any file on the machine, including secrets kept out of version control.

What a reader sees always matches the map. Each file is read from version control at the commit the map was pinned to, not from the working copy. A map edited while the server runs is picked up on the next page load.
A reader trusting a code link would be shown lines that have moved. The map would look wrong where it is right.

The file browser never presents a shortened tree as the whole project. When the skip list hid files, the tree carries a note. The note says how many files went, which pattern removed each one, and which pattern removed nothing.
A link that leaves the page may open only a known code editor. The address must start with one of a fixed list of editor schemes. A hand-typed link template using any other scheme is refused.
Without this limit a typed link template could run script inside the viewer. A reader could also be sent to an attacker's site.

The viewer page loads its two diagram libraries from the internet at exact pinned versions. Each one carries a fingerprint of the expected file. The browser refuses to run a file whose content does not match that fingerprint.
Without this check, a changed library file could run any code inside the viewer and read the project it shows.
Reads project files at a pinned commit. The map server shows each file as it was when the map was built.
Runs every coyodex command. Setup builds a private environment inside the coyodex folder, so no package lands in the machine's own Python.
Parses code in many languages. The file survey uses tree-sitter to count symbols and imports before an altitude is chosen.
Supplies the grammar for each language the survey parses. Without the pack no non-Python file can be surveyed.
Runs the coyodex test suite. Only a coyodex developer installs pytest.
